_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 3 Forward, Back, Left, Right. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (four instructions; Robo on the grid; a turn is not a move; a program for Robo; predict first; test it, fix it), in the lesson's own words and on the lesson's own grid: 5 columns by 4 rows, Robo with its yellow arrow, the flower, a wall. The Computing kit keeps Robo's grid inside an activity closure, so the film DRAWS the grid itself in the engine's idiom and takes the RULES from ART.robo - the four facings, the two turn tables, the angles and the four commands - so no route here can disagree with the lesson's own.
title: Forward, Back, Left, Right
subtitle: Grade 1 Computing
objectives: Know how to give simple instructions, using directional language (forward, backwards, left, right), to navigate a path.
Know that the order of instructions is important when creating algorithms.
Know how to recreate algorithms as programs to perform simple tasks.
Predict what is likely to happen when programs are run.
Know how to run programs to test whether they produce the desired result.

beats.say: Robo is a robot on a grid of squares. It only does what it is told.
You give it four instructions: forward, backwards, turn left, turn right.
Robo knows four instructions, and only four. Here they are.
Forward moves Robo one square the way it is facing.
Backwards moves it one square the other way, without turning round.
Turn left spins Robo to its left. It stays on the same square.
Turn right spins it the other way. Now Robo faces right again.
Here is Robo on the grid. The flower is what it must reach.
The yellow arrow shows which way Robo is facing. Look at it first.
Forward moves Robo one square the way the arrow points.
Turn left. The arrow spins round, and Robo stays on its square.
Now forward goes up the grid, because Robo is facing a new way.

scenes.heading: A turn is not a move

beats.say: A turn arrow spins Robo on the spot. It moves nowhere at all.
A forward arrow sends it one square. Those are two different jobs.
Count a turn as a square, and Robo stops one square short.

at.count: Count a turn as a square

beats.say: So look at the arrow every time. Turn first, then move.
First count the squares to the flower. Two across, then two up.
Now tap the arrows. The list you build is called a program.
Press Go. Robo runs one instruction at a time, and reaches the flower.
The order matters. Put the turn first, and Robo ends up somewhere else.
Robo also stops early if it bumps into a wall. Bump!
A good programmer knows where Robo will stop before pressing Go.
That is called predicting. Read the program with your finger.
Forward, forward. Your finger goes up two squares.
Turn right. The arrow points a new way, but your finger does not move.
One more forward, and your finger lands on the flower. Now press Go.
Test another program. This time Robo stops beside the flower, not on it.
So the program is not right yet. Read it again, slowly.
There is one forward too many. Take that one away.
Press Go again. Robo lands on the flower. Programmers do this all day.
Forward, backwards, turn left and turn right. Those are the four.
A list of them is a program, and the order matters every time.
Predict where Robo stops. Then press Go, and fix what went wrong.
